query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the key mechanism governing simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion is the in situ formation of a stable, fine-grained, and chemically homogeneous passive oxide film at the surface—promoted by minor additions of refractory elements such as Mo—which not only strengthens the subsurface microstructure but also forms a continuous barrier that resists corrosive attack and retards wear-induced mechanical degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a base composition such as CoCrFeNi with a controlled minor addition of Mo (or similar refractory/passivating element) exhibiting a homogeneous single-phase microstructure with moderate grain size.
generation.intervention: Introduce/Reformulate the alloy by increasing the refractory element content (e.g., Mo) that favors the formation of a stable oxide during service and promotes grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Testing in a combined wear–corrosion environment (e.g., sliding wear tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature), where mechanical stresses and corrosive agents act simultaneously.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, fine-grained passive oxide film at the contact interface; facilitated by grain refinement and lattice distortion from Mo addition.
generation.mechanism: Under simultaneous mechanical wear and chemical attack, the refractory element promotes the rapid formation and maintenance of a continuous, adherent oxide film that acts as a physical barrier (limiting oxygen and Cl– ingress) and also reduces friction by reinforcing the near-surface microstructure. This film reduces both the corrosion current (by lowering the electrochemical activity) and the wear rate (by restraining abrasive particle formation and microcracking).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline alloy lacking the enhanced Mo content, the modified HEA is predicted to exhibit lower combined degradation rates with a measurable reduction in both wear volume loss and corrosion current density. The alloy with the stable oxide film should maintain lower friction coefficients and more durable passive behavior under cyclic wear–corrosion exposure.
generation.baseline: A composition of the same base alloy but with lower or no Mo (or equivalent passivating element) addition, which does not favor robust passive film formation.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected to hold in environments where oxide passivation is viable (temperatures that allow oxide formation and in neutral chloride solutions at modest temperatures) but might fail in extremes (e.g., very high temperatures or highly reducing environments that destabilize the oxide layer).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in wear and corrosion rates remains uncertain due to potential interplay with environmental variables (e.g., pH, temperature) and the scale of microstructural refinement achieved. The long-term stability of the passive film under cyclic mechanical loads is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on identical substrates: one with the enhanced Mo addition (or equivalent refractory element intended to promote passivation) and one baseline without the addition. Subject both sets to standardized sliding wear tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. Characterize the surface film formation via cross-sectional microscopy and electrochemical tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) both before and after wear. Measure friction coefficients, wear volume loss, and corrosion current densities over repeated cycles.
measurements: Surface morphology and passive film continuity (via SEM/EDS)
Grain size and phase homogeneity (via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with enhanced Mo addition fails to form a continuous passive oxide film (as observed via microscopy) and does not exhibit significant reductions in wear volume loss, friction coefficient, and corrosion current density compared to the baseline, the hypothesis that the stable passive film mediates combined wear–corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
